title: Finale

jokes.text: Nobody buys DVDs anymore. / It'll be a pledge gift.
jokes.setup: The documentary crew announces they're getting bonus footage for the DVD.
jokes.punchline: Dwight points out nobody buys DVDs, and the crew's response—it's a PBS pledge gift—is somehow even more pathetic.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical opener. The escalating logic—DVDs are dead, but don't worry, it's a PBS pledge gift—doubles the joke. Dwight's skepticism of the whole enterprise is character-specific and sets the meta tone of the finale well.

jokes.text: PBS. The propaganda wing of Bill and Melinda Gates, and viewers like you.
jokes.setup: The crew explains it's a PBS production.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's conspiratorial take on PBS as a propaganda operation, immediately undercut by the gentle PBS pledge-drive tagline 'and viewers like you.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptionally well-crafted. The joke has two distinct layers: Dwight's paranoid conspiracy framing and the whiplash pivot to the affectionate 'and viewers like you' which is a straight PBS slogan. The juxtaposition is jarring and perfect. Deeply Dwight-specific—only he would describe PBS as a propaganda wing and then accidentally quote its own heartwarming tagline. Highly quotable, original concept.

jokes.text: Dwight fires Kevin via cake frosting that reads 'Get out'
jokes.setup: Office farewell cakes are being distributed. Kevin expects a celebration cake.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's cake reads 'Get out'—Dwight is using the cake ceremony to fire him.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout gags. Firing someone via cake frosting is a perfectly Dwight-brained solution—bureaucratic cruelty delivered with festive packaging. The slow reveal ('Go ahead and just read the frosting') and Kevin's genuine confusion make it land hard. The line 'The cake has spoken, Pam. Sorry' is a gem of absurdist character comedy. Earns its score because it's grounded in who Dwight is.

jokes.text: 'Get out'? What does that mean? / It's a colloquial way of saying you're fired, Kevin. Which you are.
jokes.setup: Kevin reads his cake and is confused.
jokes.punchline: Dwight explains 'get out' is a colloquialism for being fired, with bureaucratic calm.
jokes.explanation: The follow-through on joke #3. Dwight defining 'get out' as a colloquialism for being fired—delivered with the gravity of a HR manual—is perfectly economical. Kevin's obliviousness and Dwight's clinical explanation are an ideal character pairing.

jokes.text: The cake has spoken, Pam. Sorry.
jokes.setup: Pam protests that Dwight can't fire Kevin via cake.
jokes.punchline: Dwight treats the cake as a binding legal authority.
jokes.explanation: The single best line in the Kevin-firing sequence. 'The cake has spoken' is an instant classic—it treats a frosted baked good as an unimpeachable legal oracle. Maximum comedy per word, uniquely Dwight, and immediately quotable. The apologetic 'Sorry' at the end adds a chef's kiss of mock-politeness. This is the kind of line that gets quoted in The Office circles for years.

jokes.text: Well, if anyone here can make a case for Kevin staying... Based on his merit. Oh. Um... I'm good.
jokes.setup: Dwight opens the floor to defend Kevin's employment.
jokes.punchline: Complete silence—no one can think of anything, and someone quietly gives up with 'I'm good.'
jokes.explanation: A well-executed awkward silence beat. The 'based on his merit' qualifier is the real knife. The collective inability of Kevin's coworkers and supposed friends to defend him is both sad and hilarious. Classic Office cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Well, Toby will stop it. Any time anyone's ever been fired, Toby's blocked it, so... Yeah. Yeah, I don't think... Toby, wait, wait. Hold that thought. Here's your cake.
jokes.setup: Pam hopes Toby will block the firing as HR always does. Toby starts to speak up.
jokes.punchline: Dwight cuts off Toby mid-thought by firing him too, handing him a 'get out' cake.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant callback and escalation. The show has spent nine seasons establishing Toby as the hapless HR foil who Michael loathed. Dwight using the one moment Toby tries to do his job as the moment to fire him is a perfectly earned payoff. The cake mechanism being reused immediately gives it running-gag energy. Structurally excellent—Pam's setup line makes us think Toby will save the day, then Dwight pulls the rug.

jokes.text: Bye, bye, Toby — Toby walking out with his 'get out' cake
jokes.setup: Toby has just been fired while trying to help Kevin.
jokes.punchline: The visual of Toby shuffling out with his firing cake, a callback to Kevin's humiliation just moments before.
jokes.explanation: The visual punctuation on the Toby firing joke. Toby's hapless exit with his humiliation cake in hand is a perfect image. The singsong 'Bye, bye, Toby' adds a final twist of cruelty. Effective running-gag payoff.

jokes.text: At least I got chocolate.
jokes.setup: Toby has just been fired via cake.
jokes.punchline: His only consolation is that his firing cake is chocolate flavor.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best single lines. Toby's capacity for pathetic acceptance of his own humiliation is a nine-season character note played to perfection here. The line is so economical—five words—and so perfectly in character that it feels inevitable in retrospect. 'At least I got chocolate' is the Toby epitaph. Highly quotable, deeply earned.

jokes.text: I bike to work now. It saves on gas, it's cheaper than a vasectomy, and, oh, yeah, it's good for the environment, too.
jokes.setup: Ryan is explaining his new lifestyle choices in a talking head.
jokes.punchline: He lists biking's benefits in descending order of rationality, burying the environmental benefit after 'cheaper than a vasectomy.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating logic—gas savings, cheaper than vasectomy, oh right environment—is Ryan's voice exactly. His self-absorbed priority ordering, where birth control economics outranks environmentalism, is perfect character comedy. The vasectomy non-sequitur is bizarre enough to get a genuine laugh.

jokes.text: Dwight is imitating Japanese business practices, for reasons he explained to us in Japanese.
jokes.setup: Jim is giving a where-are-they-now update on office members.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's reason for imitating Japanese practices is that he explained it in Japanese—implying no one understood and no one pushed back.
jokes.explanation: Efficient and funny. The joke is that Dwight's eccentricities have become so normalized that no one even bothers to ask for clarification—especially when it's in a language they don't understand. Jim's deadpan delivery sells it. Good economy.

jokes.text: Ugh. Look at Meredith. She's disgusting. Those feet. They're like the paws of an orangutan.
jokes.setup: Angela says her heart is open and she's at peace moments before this.
jokes.punchline: Immediately after professing inner peace, she attacks Meredith's feet.
jokes.explanation: The irony works well—Angela's spiritual proclamation is debunked in seconds. 'Paws of an orangutan' is a good specific insult. The structure (peace claim → immediate cruelty) is a classic sitcom beat, but the specificity of the orangutan feet elevates it slightly above generic Angela-is-judgmental humor.

jokes.text: I think she looks good. Now that she's wearing sports bras, we don't see her boobs as much.
jokes.setup: Angela has just savaged Meredith's appearance.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis defends Meredith by pointing out the one improvement: fewer visible boobs. Phrased as a sincere compliment.
jokes.explanation: Phyllis's left-handed compliment is perfectly in character—cheerfully oblivious to how backhanded it is. The joke works because she's genuinely trying to be kind and accidentally making it worse. Good character specificity.

jokes.text: Oh, and the old man to feed us the cheese that he's been fermenting since the day of my birth. You keep forgetting about him. I don't know why.
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight discuss who needs to be at the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Dwight casually mentions a man fermenting birth-cheese as a wedding tradition, irritated that Jim keeps forgetting about him.
jokes.explanation: The Schrute birth-cheese fermenter is a fantastic piece of world-building absurdism. The irritation that Jim keeps forgetting this important figure—as if birth-cheese fermenters are something you should easily remember—is the perfect character-comedy angle. Dwight's bafflement at Jim's confusion is funnier than any direct joke about the cheese itself.

jokes.text: I always liked Devon. I hired him back after Creed faked his own death in the baler the day after the doc aired.
jokes.setup: Dwight explains personnel changes at Dunder Mifflin.
jokes.punchline: Creed faked his own death in the office baler—a criminally insane detail delivered as a mundane HR note.
jokes.explanation: Creed faking his death in the baler is exactly the kind of dark, absurd Creed-lore payoff the show has been building toward for nine seasons. The matter-of-fact delivery makes it funnier. 'The only person he fooled was Kevin' and 'then the police showed up' extend it beautifully.

jokes.text: Turns out Creed was in the band The Grass Roots, in the 1960s. During that time, the police say he sold drugs. And trafficked in endangered species meat. And stole weapons-grade LSD from the military.
jokes.setup: Dwight explains why the police came after Creed faked his death.
jokes.punchline: Each item in Creed's criminal history is more unhinged than the last, culminating in 'weapons-grade LSD from the military.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating Creed crimes list is among the episode's funniest moments and one of the best Creed jokes in the entire series. The structure is flawless: drugs (plausible for a '60s rock musician), endangered species meat (a jump), weapons-grade LSD from the military (completely unhinged). Each item lands separately and together they build to an absurdist crescendo that perfectly caps nine years of Creed mystery. The parenthetical 'the police say' treats it as credible law-enforcement information, adding deadpan weight. A genuine standout.

jokes.text: Party time, whorehouse.
jokes.setup: Jim tells everyone to be ready for the bachelor party limo.
jokes.punchline: Andy enthusiastically suggests a whorehouse as their destination.
jokes.explanation: Functional. Andy's eagerness and poor social calibration are well-established, but this is a fairly cheap laugh—the humor comes from the word 'whorehouse' more than any real comedic craft.

jokes.text: Dwight has made me his bestisch Mensch, which is Schrute for 'best man.' He is putting himself entirely in my hands tonight, and I know, for over 12 years, I've done nothing but trick and prank him. But tonight? Only good surprises.
jokes.setup: Jim explains his role as bestisch Mensch and his history of pranking Dwight.
jokes.punchline: The irony that Jim—the architect of a decade of Dwight pranks—is now vowing to deliver only good surprises, while we already suspect he's planning something.
jokes.explanation: Solid setup for the evening's arc. 'Bestisch Mensch' being Schrute for 'best man' is a nice small gag. The talking head works as dramatic irony—we know Jim is planning pranks—but the joke itself is more structural than laugh-out-loud funny.

jokes.text: Often times in Hollywood portrayals of bachelor parties, there are accidental murders. That won't be necessary tonight.
jokes.setup: Dwight and Jim are discussing the bachelor party itinerary.
jokes.punchline: Dwight preemptively rules out accidental murder as a bachelor party activity, implying he considered it.
jokes.explanation: Funny and well-constructed. Dwight treating accidental bachelor party murder as a cliché to be noted and ruled out—rather than something no normal person would consider—is deeply character-specific. 'That won't be necessary tonight' implies a cost-benefit analysis was performed.

jokes.text: Great, now we've got three hours to fill.
jokes.setup: Dwight rules out accidental murder from the itinerary.
jokes.punchline: Jim's deadpan reaction that eliminating murder from a bachelor party opens up a problematic time gap.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jim deadpan. By playing along with the premise—treating murder as a legitimate time-filling activity whose absence creates a scheduling problem—Jim sells the absurdist logic of the world. Short, punchy, and effective.

jokes.text: Mose has been weird? That's so unlike him.
jokes.setup: Dwight mentions Mose has been acting weird since Angela moved in.
jokes.punchline: Jim's mock-surprise that Mose—who previously slept at the foot of Dwight's bed—is behaving unusually.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient Jim sarcasm beat that rewards viewers who remember Mose's long history of being profoundly strange. The more you know about Mose, the funnier this lands. Good economy.

jokes.text: America's Next A Cappella Sensation aired my audition, and when I started sobbing uncontrollably, apparently, that struck a chord with quite a lot of people. Not a very compassionate chord.
jokes.setup: Andy explains what happened after his a cappella audition breakdown.
jokes.punchline: 'Not a very compassionate chord'—Andy acknowledges people found his breakdown funny rather than moving.
jokes.explanation: 'Not a very compassionate chord' is a lovely wordplay-adjacent self-aware line. Andy's gradual, painful self-awareness about his humiliation is great character work, and this line shows he understands exactly what happened while still being mortified. The music pun is earned because he's talking about an a cappella show.

jokes.text: One from the Philippines got 12 million hits.
jokes.setup: Andy explains his cry video going viral and inspiring parodies.
jokes.punchline: The Filipino parody—of Andy crying at an audition—got more views than the original, adding insult to injury.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective escalation. The specificity of 'the Philippines' and '12 million' makes it funnier than a vague 'went even more viral.' Andy's matter-of-fact delivery of his own international humiliation is on-brand.

jokes.text: Aw, come on, Baby Wawa. Don't be such a baby.
jokes.setup: Andy explains that late night shows made fun of his viral crying clip.
jokes.punchline: The clip of a TV host taunting Andy with the nickname 'Baby Wawa' — cruel and reductive, landing as dark comedy.
jokes.explanation: 'Baby Wawa' is a good nickname and the mock-sympathy 'don't be such a baby' layering is funny. More of a solid joke than an exceptional one—the comedy relies somewhat on the accumulated cringe of Andy's situation.

jokes.text: For Weekend Update, I'm Seth Meyers! That's Baby Wawa! Good night!
jokes.setup: Andy's humiliation has reached national TV.
jokes.punchline: Seth Meyers signs off Weekend Update by spotlighting Andy's 'Baby Wawa' nickname as the comedic centerpiece of his segment.
jokes.explanation: The SNL cameo is a fun real-world cross-pollination that emphasizes the scale of Andy's humiliation. Functional meta-comedy, though it relies on celebrity cameo value as much as writing craft.

jokes.text: After my clip blew up, I actually got a call from the Double Rainbow guy and the fat Star Wars kid. Turns out they have a support group. Not really my scene.
jokes.setup: Andy's viral humiliation made him internet famous.
jokes.punchline: The viral-fame support group existing is funny; Andy declining to join because it's 'not really my scene' implies he considers himself above it—despite clearly suffering the same fate.
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. The specificity of referencing the Double Rainbow guy and the fat Star Wars kid gives it grounding in real internet culture. Andy's class-conscious rejection of the support group—as if he's too sophisticated for viral victims—is a perfect character beat. The line 'not really my scene' does a lot of heavy lifting.

jokes.text: That's the reason Kevin got fired. It's his magic number. He used to call it a 'keleven.' He told Dwight, 'A mistake plus keleven gets you home by 7:00.' He was home by 4:45 that day.
jokes.setup: A new employee notices an unexplained symbol appearing throughout the company's old accounts.
jokes.punchline: Kevin invented a fake number called 'keleven' to balance his books, and the math was so wrong he got home two-plus hours early.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Keleven' is an inspired piece of character work—Kevin inventing a number to fix his accounting errors is both perfectly Kevin and a devastating indictment of his professional life. The specificity of 'A mistake plus keleven gets you home by 7:00' as a genuine rule Kevin followed is absurdist genius. The kicker—'He was home by 4:45 that day'—is the perfect button. This joke also retroactively enriches why Kevin was fired. Exceptional craft.

jokes.text: Oh, I live in Poland now. The Scranton of the EU.
jokes.setup: Nellie appears via video or in person to give her update.
jokes.punchline: She defines Poland entirely by its similarity to Scranton—the most depressing possible frame of reference.
jokes.explanation: 'The Scranton of the EU' is a beautifully economical line. It tells us everything about Scranton (unremarkable, secondary city) and Poland's position in the EU simultaneously, in five words. Highly quotable and easy to lift out of context.

jokes.text: After Dwight fired me, I moved to New York to write the Great American Novel. I have six roommates, which are better than friends, you know, because they have to give you one month's notice before they leave.
jokes.setup: Ryan explains his post-Dunder Mifflin life in New York.
jokes.punchline: Ryan prefers roommates over friends because friends can abandon you without notice—a bleak self-aware admission about his own social isolation.
jokes.explanation: A devastating and funny Ryan joke. The logic—roommates are contractually obligated to stay, unlike friends—reveals that Ryan has no real friends and knows it. The casual way he presents this as a life hack rather than a cry for help is perfect character work. Deeply Ryan, deeply sad, very funny.

jokes.text: Little warm.
jokes.setup: Phyllis gives Andy a big hug and says she's been worried about him.
jokes.punchline: Andy's only response to a warm, sincere embrace from a maternal colleague is the understatement 'little warm'—suggesting emotional numbness or social awkwardness.
jokes.explanation: A quick, effective physical comedy beat. Andy's inability to receive warmth gracefully—reducing a heartfelt hug to a temperature complaint—is funny and slightly sad. Works within the Andy-is-broken-right-now arc.

jokes.text: Hey, man. How you doing? I didn't call 'cause I figured you changed your number. No, I didn't change the number. All good, though. Phone never rings.
jokes.setup: Andy and Darryl have an awkward reunion where Andy tries to excuse not reaching out.
jokes.punchline: Darryl confirms he never changed his number—Andy just never called—and then Darryl reveals his phone never rings anyway, accidentally making it more awkward.
jokes.explanation: A nicely layered cringe beat. Andy's excuse is immediately deflated, then Darryl's 'phone never rings' accidentally doubles the awkwardness. Small but well-observed social comedy.

jokes.text: You remember my two Lap-Band surgeries, right? Neither do I. Guten prank number one.
jokes.setup: Pam explains she and Jim made excuses every other weekend to avoid the reunion. Her excuse involves Lap-Band surgeries.
jokes.punchline: 'Neither do I'—she immediately reveals she made them up, confirming they were just avoiding the event. Jim labels it 'Guten prank number one.'
jokes.explanation: The structure is sharp—Pam asks if you remember the surgeries, then immediately undercuts it. 'Neither do I' is a great button. Jim claiming it as 'Guten prank number one' ties it into the bachelor party arc well.

jokes.text: Waazzuup!
jokes.setup: Oscar says he's going to the bachelor party with the guys and just has to remember how he acted before he came out.
jokes.punchline: His impression of pre-coming-out bro behavior is the Budweiser 'Wassup' ad. The delivery lands as both self-aware and absurd.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. The buildup—Oscar solemnly saying he needs to remember how he acted before coming out—creates the expectation of something profound. The punchline being 'Waazzuup' from a 2000 Budweiser ad is a delightfully small, specific comedy choice. The dated pop culture reference actually makes it funnier (that's the best he's got?)

jokes.text: Hey, why are we stopping? Jim, this isn't on the itinerary. Jim? Get out! Come on!
jokes.setup: The limo stops unexpectedly. Dwight is confused and slightly alarmed.
jokes.punchline: They've stopped at a field for Dwight to fire a bazooka—his delight at the reveal is immediate and enormous.
jokes.explanation: The bazooka reveal is excellent character comedy. Jim remembering that Dwight's dream is to fire a bazooka—and procuring one—is the perfect 'guten prank' because it's a genuinely kind thing to do for Dwight specifically. The reveal works because we understand immediately that this is the most Dwight gift possible.

jokes.text: A bazooka. You remembered.
jokes.setup: Dwight sees what Jim has arranged.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's quiet, almost tender 'You remembered' treats a military weapon like a sentimental gift.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most emotionally resonant funny moments. 'A bazooka. You remembered.' plays like a romantic comedy beat about a forgotten anniversary gift, but it's about a rocket launcher. The tender delivery from Dwight—a man who usually expresses affection through dominance hierarchies—makes this genuinely sweet and funny simultaneously. The economy (four words) is exceptional.

jokes.text: Hey, I know you. You going to sit here and cry?
jokes.setup: The guys arrive at a private bar room and Andy is recognized from his viral video.
jokes.punchline: The patron immediately mocks Andy with his viral nickname, undercutting any sense of normalcy.
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe beat. The recurring humiliation of Andy being recognized everywhere he goes adds to his arc, but the joke itself is just the setup for the more interesting exchange that follows.

jokes.text: I spoke at Cornell during Commencement week. Well, I mean, the seniors invited me as a joke, but it was a huge success.
jokes.setup: Andy reports things are going well—he even spoke at Cornell's commencement.
jokes.punchline: He was invited as a joke, undercut immediately, but he turned it into a genuine success.
jokes.explanation: A great two-beat joke. The first beat deflates Andy's success story (invited as a joke), but the second beat reclaims some dignity (it was a genuine success). This is a more sophisticated joke than it appears—it honors Andy's resilience while still making him the butt of the setup.

jokes.text: That's how I got my new job in the Admissions Office. Is that a volunteer program, or... No, it's a job. Things are going great!
jokes.setup: Andy explains he got a job at Cornell through his surprise commencement speech success.
jokes.punchline: Jim's reflexive assumption that it must be volunteer work—and Andy's desperate insistence that it's a real job—lands as both cringe and character comedy.
jokes.explanation: Jim's casual assumption that Andy's job is volunteer work—an unthinking insult—is classic Jim-as-unsuspecting-bad-guy energy. Andy's slightly-too-emphatic 'Things are going great!' signals his fragility. Well-observed.

jokes.text: This is my big sister, Rachael. No, this is my big sister, Angela. We're very close. We even have our own special language.
jokes.setup: Angela introduces her sister to Dwight's family at the bachelorette party.
jokes.punchline: Angela and her sister are so similar—prim, judgmental, identically cold—that they've developed their own shared language, which we then see demonstrated.
jokes.explanation: The setup for the 'special language' joke is a decent character gag. The visual of two identical Angelas communicating in cat-lady code is funnier than it reads on the page.

jokes.text: Meredith's son arriving as the bachelor party stripper
jokes.setup: A stripper arrives at the bachelor party claiming to be the 'chef's special.'
jokes.punchline: The stripper is Meredith's son—and Meredith herself is at the party.
jokes.explanation: The Meredith's-son-is-the-stripper reveal is a great structural gag. The 'chef's special' misdirection is well-executed, and the reveal that it's not just anyone's kid but Meredith's—and that Meredith is there—layers the cringe beautifully. Meredith's complete lack of shame and active encouragement is what makes it exceptional.

jokes.text: Angela, special repairman is here! / What is this? / Shut up! Jakey? / Mom?
jokes.setup: The stripper is now at the bachelorette party, announced by Meredith.
jokes.punchline: The stripper recognizes his mother at the party and calls her 'Mom.'
jokes.explanation: The callback landing at both parties—Jakey is at Angela's bachelorette too—escalates the original joke effectively. 'Mom?' in the middle of a stripper reveal is a perfect cringe beat. Meredith's unselfconscious reaction carries the scene.

jokes.text: Stripper's only as good as his song. / Yeah! Good song choice, Jakey!
jokes.setup: Meredith is watching her son strip at a party she's attending.
jokes.punchline: Meredith critiques/praises her son's music selection as if reviewing a performance—completely unfazed by the fundamental wrongness of the situation.
jokes.explanation: 'Stripper's only as good as his song' is a piece of Meredith wisdom that belongs in the pantheon of her greatest hits. Her maternal pride in her son's stripping craft is simultaneously horrifying and oddly wholesome. Only Meredith could deliver this line. One of the episode's best character-specific moments.

jokes.text: Be gentle, Jakey, gentle! / Stop it, Meredith! / Sorry! My bad. Go ahead, Jakey.
jokes.setup: Meredith is interfering with her son's stripping performance.
jokes.punchline: Meredith is physically getting involved in the performance, has to be restrained, apologizes, and then immediately encourages him to continue.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Meredith inserting herself into her son's performance is peak Meredith comedy. 'My bad. Go ahead, Jakey' is a great line—she's simultaneously apologetic and completely undeterred.

jokes.text: For the last time, I'd like a side salad with balsamic. / Dwight, for the last time, she's not a waitress. / You're telling me! / If you want her to leave, just tip her. / What for? We haven't even gotten bread yet!
jokes.setup: The stripper is performing. Dwight wants to order food.
jokes.punchline: Dwight has been persistently treating the stripper as a waitress and is furious about the service quality.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional Dwight joke. The bit that Dwight has been ordering food from the stripper—and is genuinely annoyed about the lack of bread service—is beautifully absurdist and completely in character. 'We haven't even gotten bread yet!' is one of the episode's most quotable lines. Dwight's obliviousness to the stripper's actual function, combined with his intense focus on the food service failure, is comic gold.

jokes.text: Oh, man! I never thought I'd say this but I think I ate too much bone marrow.
jokes.setup: Chaos is erupting—Angela has been kidnapped by Mose.
jokes.punchline: Darryl's only concern is that he overconsumpted bone marrow. The specificity of bone marrow (not 'food') is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The bone marrow specificity makes this line. 'I ate too much' would be nothing; 'bone marrow' elevates it to an absurdist detail. Darryl's complete detachment from the crisis—focused on his own gastrointestinal situation—is funny but not particularly character-specific for Darryl.

jokes.text: Good old Mose! They think it was Mose. Oh, great! He's getting into the spirit of the festivities. Fantastic! He just pulled off a Braut entführt.
jokes.setup: Angela has been kidnapped from the bachelorette party.
jokes.punchline: Dwight cheerfully explains that this is a traditional ceremonial bridal kidnapping (Braut entführt)—and he's delighted, not concerned.
jokes.explanation: Typical Schrute family tradition comedy—violence and kidnapping recontextualized as quaint folk customs. Dwight's delight at the tradition being enacted is perfectly in character, and the fake German tradition name ('Braut entführt') is funny in its specificity.

jokes.text: Well, well, well, well, well. That's six 'wells'. Did I get that number right, Dwight?
jokes.setup: Kevin dramatically enters his bar, doing a classic villain monologue opener with 'well, well, well.'
jokes.punchline: He loses count and has to ask Dwight if he got the number of 'wells' right—undercutting his own dramatic entrance.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. Kevin attempting a villain's entrance and immediately failing at basic counting—then humbly asking Dwight for the correct number—is the perfect Kevin joke. It captures his self-awareness (he knows the 'well, well, well' is a pose) and his fundamental limitation (math) simultaneously. The keleven joke earlier makes this land even harder as a second-act payoff on Kevin's numeracy. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, and structurally flawless.

jokes.text: Waste of a good hatchet.
jokes.setup: Jim tells Dwight it's time to bury the hatchet with Kevin.
jokes.punchline: Dwight takes the idiom literally and mourns the hypothetical waste of an actual hatchet.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Dwight literalism joke. Four words, maximum character specificity. Dwight's tool-economy mindset makes burying an actual hatchet seem genuinely wasteful to him. The resigned delivery makes it land.

jokes.text: Well... / I heard you say 'well' the first time.
jokes.setup: Dwight attempts to speak to Kevin with a dramatic 'Well...'
jokes.punchline: Kevin cuts him off—he heard it the first time—a callback to Kevin's own failed 'well, well, well' entrance.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Kevin shutting down Dwight's 'well' entrance—after his own failed multi-well entrance—creates a lovely inversion where the usually-oblivious Kevin is the one pointing out the cliché. The economy is perfect.

jokes.text: It was nothing personal. It's just that you were terrible at your job. / You're just saying that to make me feel better. / No, really. You were terrible at math, and organization, time management, personal hygiene.
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to reconcile with Kevin by explaining his firing.
jokes.punchline: Kevin mistakes Dwight's brutal catalogue of his failings for kindness—and Dwight's list is so comprehensive and specific it becomes its own joke.
jokes.explanation: The inversion—Kevin thinking a devastating list of his failures is meant to comfort him—is sharp. Dwight's unsentimental approach to reconciliation (just tell him exactly why he was terrible) is perfectly in character. The list itself (math, organization, time management, personal hygiene) is funny in its thoroughness.

jokes.text: Your Internet searches were so filthy we had to throw out your computer.
jokes.setup: Dwight is listing all of Kevin's professional failings.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's internet searches were so bad the company destroyed the hardware.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation from the previous list—adding internet searches as a failing is funny in itself, and the detail that they had to physically throw out the computer (not just wipe it, destroy it) escalates it further. Pure Kevin.

jokes.text: Is that all it was? / That's it.
jokes.setup: Dwight has just listed Kevin's many catastrophic professional failings.
jokes.punchline: Kevin, relieved, asks if that's really all—treating a devastating list of failures as reassuringly short.
jokes.explanation: The button on the reconciliation scene. Kevin's genuine relief that the list wasn't longer is both sweet and absurd. 'That's it' from Dwight—delivered with finality—implies there could have been more. Great economy.

jokes.text: Guten prank. / Yes, Mose. / Guten prank number three.
jokes.setup: The Dwight/Kevin reconciliation has been arranged by Jim and facilitated by Mose's bridal kidnapping.
jokes.punchline: Jim and Mose quietly share the moment, and Mose's 'Guten prank number three' confirms the kidnapping was a coordinated good prank.
jokes.explanation: A nice structural payoff on the guten pranken running gag. The reveal that Mose was in on it all along adds depth. The delivery of 'Guten prank number three' by Mose—who barely speaks—is a good beat.

jokes.text: And her legs are still numb from being in the trunk.
jokes.setup: Asked if Angela is coming, Dwight explains they can't see each other before the wedding.
jokes.punchline: He casually adds that her legs are numb from Mose keeping her in a car trunk—mentioned with zero concern.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's nonchalance about his fiancée's trunk-induced paralysis is perfectly Schrute. The dark detail is delivered as a minor inconvenience rather than a health concern. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: The man who delivered my divorce papers came by fan boat, which was kind of fun.
jokes.setup: Stanley describes his retirement life in Florida.
jokes.punchline: His divorce was delivered by fan boat—and the fun part was the boat, not the circumstances.
jokes.explanation: One of Stanley's best jokes in the episode. The casual mention of his divorce is undercut by genuine pleasure at the fan boat delivery—Stanley's priorities (fan boat > divorce trauma) are perfectly captured. The 'which was kind of fun' sells it completely. Highly quotable and deeply Stanley-specific.

jokes.text: I guess this was worth being filmed nonstop for nine years.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam feel invisible at the panel as nobody seems to care about them.
jokes.punchline: The sarcastic acknowledgment that nine years of filming was worth it for this moment of being ignored.
jokes.explanation: Functional meta-commentary on the show's relationship with its subjects. Works as a moment of dry self-awareness but isn't particularly crafted beyond the irony.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, guys. This is probably on me. I got hated on pretty hard when that auto-tune went viral.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam feel the panel ignores them while the audience focuses on other characters.
jokes.punchline: Andy takes the blame—not because of any genuine connection to their situation but because his own viral humiliation has made the whole evening about him.
jokes.explanation: Andy's self-centered framing of their invisibility—it's his fault because of his viral moment—is character-consistent and mildly funny.

jokes.text: Yeah, people hate you. / I'll go talk to the manager.
jokes.setup: Andy's viral auto-tune song is playing on the jukebox at Kevin's bar, and he notes none of the money goes to Andy.
jokes.punchline: Darryl flatly confirms people hate Andy, and Jim immediately pivots to practical problem-solving (going to the manager).
jokes.explanation: Darryl's blunt honesty is a good character note, and Jim's pivot to problem-solving (rather than comfort) is funny. Short and functional.

jokes.text: How did it feel to see your lives played out on TV? / It's like seeing a documentary about how your food is made. / It's kind of disgusting. / You learn a lot, but I didn't want to know any of it.
jokes.setup: A panel audience member asks about watching yourself on a documentary.
jokes.punchline: Creed's response—comparing it to a food documentary—is both insightful and deeply unsettling given what we know about Creed's criminal past.
jokes.explanation: The food documentary metaphor is genuinely good observational comedy—accurate and slightly gross. But it's exponentially funnier coming from Creed, who has just been revealed to be a drug dealer, endangered species meat trafficker, and military LSD thief. His insight that you 'learn a lot but didn't want to know any of it' is a perfect meta-commentary on his own criminal history being exposed.

jokes.text: With today's modern surveillance technology, we are in a constant state of being watched, whether it's our government or the government of other countries, a.k.a. Google. You guys are being filmed way more than we ever were.
jokes.setup: The panel discusses being filmed by a documentary crew.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's conspiracy-minded riff on surveillance, culminating in 'the government of other countries, a.k.a. Google.'
jokes.explanation: A strong Dwight moment. The reclassification of Google as a foreign government is a great character-specific paranoid insight. Dwight's seamless transition from legitimate surveillance concerns to treating Google as a geopolitical power is funny and recognizably him.

jokes.text: With today's modern surveillance technology, we are in a constant state of being watched, whether it's our government or the government of other countries, a.k.a. Google. You guys are being filmed way more than we ever were.
jokes.setup: Dwight follows Oscar's comment about being filmed.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's paranoid conspiracy framing of Google as 'the government of other countries' while simultaneously making the valid point about modern surveillance.
jokes.explanation: Good Dwight paranoia in the panel setting — the Google parenthetical is the specific funny detail. The broader point is actually valid (irony of the surveillance society), which makes Dwight's paranoid framing funnier by proximity.

jokes.text: Uh, no one recognizes me, but now all my friends call me Plop. So, thanks, PBS.
jokes.setup: Panel members discuss how their lives have been affected by being in the documentary.
jokes.punchline: Pete's only takeaway from nine years of filming is a nickname he doesn't want.
jokes.explanation: A small, nicely observed joke about the arbitrary nature of minor celebrity. 'Thanks, PBS' is a good button. Pete being a background character whose only documentary legacy is an unflattering nickname is funny and a little sad.

jokes.text: Jim, that DVD in the last episode was so romantic. And I think we'd all love to know, Pam, what romantic thing did you do to pay Jim back for leaving Athlead?
jokes.setup: A panel audience member asks what Pam did to pay Jim back.
jokes.punchline: The question implies Jim sacrificed everything for Pam and she owes him—creating an awkward public reckoning for their private marriage.
jokes.explanation: More of a dramatic setup than a joke itself, but the audience member's presumptuous question creates real cringe discomfort. The comedy is in the inappropriateness of airing this publicly.

jokes.text: All I can say is, if I had Jim, he'd have a free pass to do anything. I mean if I lucked into that, he could do anything. Anything. / I'm sorry, is there a question? / Uh... No.
jokes.setup: A female audience member is asked what she thought about Jim and Pam.
jokes.punchline: She delivers an increasingly breathless declaration of desire for Jim until the moderator asks for a question—which she doesn't have.
jokes.explanation: The bit of a fan publicly expressing inappropriate desire for a documentary subject—to his wife's face—is well-executed cringe comedy. 'Uh... No' as the punchline is perfectly deflating. The threefold 'Anything. Anything. Anything.' escalation is good structure.

jokes.text: Pam, what was in the teapot letter? / I think I would rather keep that private. / If you've been filmed for nine years of your life, there'd be some things that you just want to keep to yourself. / I hear you. What did it say?
jokes.setup: An audience member asks about the contents of Jim's iconic teapot letter.
jokes.punchline: Pam gives a sincere, reasonable answer about privacy—which the moderator immediately ignores by asking anyway.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured cringe joke. Pam's eloquent answer about privacy earns audience sympathy, making the moderator's immediate re-asking funnier and more outrageous. The joke is on the moderator's professional failure—pretending to hear her while not actually listening. Clean structure.

jokes.text: Do you find that your life feels pointless now that nobody's actually filming you anymore? / Yes.
jokes.setup: A panel audience member asks a rude question about post-documentary life.
jokes.punchline: Toby immediately agrees that yes, his life feels pointless.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest moments. The setup is a cruel question; the punchline is Toby's instant, sincere agreement. Nine seasons of Toby being a pathetic, overlooked presence make this land as both a laugh and a gut-punch. The single word 'Yes' is the whole joke—the fastest possible answer to the bleakest possible question. Near-perfect Toby comedy.

jokes.text: I've got a beef with that. For the first seven years I was getting my PhD in school psychology and they didn't show it. Yes, I was getting hammered, but, hey, it was college.
jokes.setup: Panel members discuss how accurately they were portrayed in the documentary.
jokes.punchline: Meredith's complaint isn't that the documentary showed her being a drunk—it's that it didn't show her getting a PhD simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character moments. The misdirection is excellent—we expect Meredith to complain about her drinking being shown, but she's upset they didn't show her academic achievement. 'Yes, I was getting hammered, but, hey, it was college' is a perfect Meredith line—simultaneously defending the drinking and contextualizing it as normal. The PhD twist is a great character revelation that makes everything about Meredith funnier retroactively.

jokes.text: Like Harry Potter? / Yeah. Like Harry Potter.
jokes.setup: Pam has just delivered a moving, earnest speech about her relationship with Jim feeling like a book you never want to end.
jokes.punchline: An audience member reduces her heartfelt metaphor to Harry Potter. And Pam just agrees.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully timed deflation of an earnest moment. Pam builds a genuine emotional crescendo and an audience member reduces it to a kids' book franchise. But Pam's 'Yeah. Like Harry Potter'—her immediate, graceful capitulation—makes it work as both funny and oddly sweet. The economy is exceptional. One of the most quotable moments in the episode.

jokes.text: So, my question is, um, don't you hate her? I mean, I would just imagine that you are so angry at her that you would hate her.
jokes.setup: A panel audience member asks Erin about her search for her birth mother.
jokes.punchline: The 'question' is just the audience member projecting intense anger onto Erin's situation, unprompted and without evidence.
jokes.explanation: The aggressively leading 'question' from the audience member is a good cringe bit. The comedy is in the questioner's weird emotional investment. Setup for the stronger Erin response that follows.

jokes.text: Maybe sometimes. But not like hate-hate. More just like, 'Mom, I hate you,' and then she would say, 'Go to your room, young lady,' and I'd stamp my foot and run upstairs. And I have a room, which is really cool.
jokes.setup: Erin is asked about hating her birth mother she's never met.
jokes.punchline: Erin imagines a mundane teenage argument with the mother she's never met, complete with foot-stamping—and then lands on 'I have a room, which is really cool' as a genuine revelation.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Erin character writing. She imagines a totally domestic argument with an imaginary mother—foot-stamp and all—and the detail that having a room would be 'really cool' cuts to the heart of her orphan experience. It's simultaneously funny (the specificity of the foot stamp) and genuinely moving. The joke earns its emotional weight completely. 'I have a room, which is really cool' is one of the episode's most quietly devastating lines.

jokes.text: Erin, same question, but about your dad? / [Erin's birth mother has just been revealed in the audience]
jokes.setup: Erin has just had an incredibly emotional, tearful reunion with her birth mother.
jokes.punchline: The moderator, immediately after the moment, asks if she also hates her dad—completely missing the emotional register of the room.
jokes.explanation: Perfect tonal whiplash. After an emotionally overwhelming moment, the moderator's pivot to the birth father question—using the same rote 'same question, but...' phrasing—is a fantastic piece of cringe comedy. The contrast between the gravity of the moment and the moderator's professional obliviousness is the whole joke.

jokes.text: Well, this feels like a good place to stop. Let's thank all our wonderful panelists for being here on this wonderful panel today.
jokes.setup: The moderator has just made a spectacular social error by immediately asking about Erin's dad.
jokes.punchline: Scrambling to recover, she lands on a banal sign-off—calling everything 'wonderful' twice—which reads as either oblivious or desperate.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'wonderful' is a nice touch—the moderator reaching for superlatives while the room is in chaos. Competent comic button but not remarkable on its own.

jokes.text: Hi. I'm Dakota. / Jeff Bomondo. / I sell ceramic tile out of Newark. / My wife's name is Kathryn. / I can show you my social security card if it helps.
jokes.setup: A man approaches at the wedding, presumably to give a gift. Dwight treats him as a potential threat requiring identity verification.
jokes.punchline: The man provides increasingly irrelevant personal information—ceramic tile, Newark, wife's name—culminating in offering his social security card.
jokes.explanation: A good Dwight-security-theater joke. The escalating personal details the man volunteers—trying desperately to seem legitimate—suggests Dwight's interrogation style is so intimidating that people offer their social security numbers voluntarily. The specificity of 'ceramic tile out of Newark' is funny on its own.

jokes.text: Can you imagine if I'd worn my Jimmy Choos? I just saved you 600 bucks, mister.
jokes.setup: Angela navigates muddy wedding grounds.
jokes.punchline: She reframes her sensible footwear choice as a financial service to her husband.
jokes.explanation: Functional character joke. Angela's materialistic self-congratulation is recognizable, but this is a fairly generic beat—similar versions could appear in many shows.

jokes.text: Whose baby is this? Oh, are you, like, a manny now? / No, this little guy is mine. / So, I was dating this girl, and one day she went out to get a new charger for her e-cigarette. Never came back. / Oldest story in the book.
jokes.setup: Kelly sees Ryan with a baby she doesn't recognize.
jokes.punchline: The mother of Ryan's child abandoned him to get an e-cigarette charger and never returned. Kelly calls it 'the oldest story in the book.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The e-cigarette charger as the reason for abandonment is a perfect modern-specific detail—both extremely mundane and extremely Ryan. Kelly calling it 'the oldest story in the book' is the perfect button, treating modern ghosting as ancient tragedy. The joke rewards both Ryan and Kelly fans equally. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: No, Kelly, he is not named after a hip-hop artist from 2011. It's Drake, like a mix of Drew and Blake.
jokes.setup: Kelly is excited about Ryan's baby being named Drake, assuming it's after the rapper.
jokes.punchline: Ryan has merged two WASPy frat names into a worse, also-trendy name—while thinking he's being original.
jokes.explanation: A great character comedy joke. Ryan's attempt to be original—naming his son after a portmanteau of Drew and Blake—is so aggressively WASPy it loops back around to being just as zeitgeist-chasing as naming him after Drake the rapper. The joke captures Ryan's oblivious pretension perfectly. 'From 2011' is a nice dig at the datedness of the reference.

jokes.text: Ravi's a pediatrician, and some of his patients are total uggos. / Uh, they're called premature, sweetie.
jokes.setup: Kelly is explaining Ravi's medical practice.
jokes.punchline: Kelly describes premature babies as 'uggos' (ugly). Ravi corrects her with the medical and moral terminology.
jokes.explanation: A compact, effective Kelly joke. Her superficiality reaching into medical terminology is perfectly in character—she'd evaluate a NICU on the same basis as a photo shoot. Ravi's gentle correction ('they're called premature, sweetie') is the ideal straight-man response. High economy.

jokes.text: Oh, boy. Maybe your heels are too high. / No, my heels aren't too high. / It's because I spent three hours in a car trunk.
jokes.setup: Angela stumbles at the wedding.
jokes.punchline: She corrects the assumption that her heels are the problem—she's impaired because Mose kept her in a car trunk for three hours.
jokes.explanation: A good callback. Angela's correction—it's not the heels, it's the trunk—is both a callback to the kidnapping and a perfect character note (she's defensive about her footwear choices while completely normalizing having been in a trunk). Well-executed.

jokes.text: The minister just told me that it's tradition for the bestisch Mensch to be older than the groom. Oh, come on. I've never heard of such a thing. I haven't heard of it, obviously.
jokes.setup: Jim tells Dwight he can't be bestisch Mensch because of an age-related tradition.
jokes.punchline: Dwight quickly acknowledges he's never heard of this—because Jim is making it up, and even Dwight can tell.
jokes.explanation: A solid setup for the Michael reveal. Dwight's 'I haven't heard of it, obviously' shows he's aware this is a prank—which makes his willingness to play along (for the sake of whatever Jim has planned) touching. Good structural function.

jokes.text: I can't believe you came! / That's what she said.
jokes.setup: Michael Scott appears at the wedding—a complete surprise. Dwight's overwhelmed reaction is 'I can't believe you came!'
jokes.punchline: Michael's first words back on the show after seasons away: 'That's what she said.'
jokes.explanation: The single greatest joke of the episode and one of the best jokes in The Office's entire run. Michael's return is already an emotional event for viewers. The fact that Dwight's genuine emotional exclamation—'I can't believe you came!'—is the perfect setup for Michael's signature joke, delivered as his first words after seasons away, is structurally flawless. It's earned by nine seasons of the show. It works as a real 'that's what she said' setup AND as the ultimate callback to the Michael Scott era. The economy is perfect (four words). It generates simultaneous laughter and tears. This is what a 9.5 looks like on craft—it would be a 10 if the setup weren't slightly convenient, but even that convenience is part of the joy.

jokes.text: As is traditional to the Schrutes, the lovers are standing in their own graves, as a reminder that this is the only escape from what they are about to do. / See, I get what they're trying to do, but why are the graves so shallow?
jokes.setup: Dwight and Angela stand in graves dug into the earth at their wedding.
jokes.punchline: Jim gets the symbolism—marriage as inescapable as death—but is distracted by the practical question of grave depth.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Schrute wedding absurdism. The tradition itself is darkly funny (marriage = death). Jim's reaction—getting the symbolism but fixating on the grave's structural inadequacy—is the perfect best-man beat. 'See, I get what they're trying to do' shows Jim has fully accepted Schrute weirdness after years of exposure, and his practical concern about shallow graves is a great character note.

jokes.text: Release the doves! [Vultures fly out]
jokes.setup: At the conclusion of the wedding ceremony, Dwight announces the release of doves.
jokes.punchline: What are released are not doves but vultures—either by mistake or as another Schrute tradition.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed visual gag. The expectation of romantic doves—a wedding cliché—is subverted by vultures, which are simultaneously wrong (for a wedding) and deeply right (for a Schrute wedding). The fact that Dwight doesn't seem surprised suggests this may have been intentional, which makes it funnier. The crowd's horrified reaction is the payoff. Economy is excellent—the setup is one sentence, the subversion is one image.

jokes.text: Now, please take your hay bales to the reception. They'll be used for seating. Complimentary hay hooks are placed along the aisles. Just stab them on in there.
jokes.setup: The wedding ceremony concludes and guests are directed to the reception.
jokes.punchline: Seating at the Schrute wedding is hay bales with complimentary hay hooks—guests are instructed to stab the hay hooks 'on in there.'
jokes.explanation: Good Schrute world-building comedy. Hay hooks as wedding accessories are funny in themselves; 'just stab them on in there' as gentle instruction is the perfect casual touch of farm-implement violence. Dwight providing hay hooks as complimentary items implies advance planning.

jokes.text: Michael has so many pictures of his kids, he had to get two phones with two numbers, and he pays two bills. / He's just so happy to have a family plan.
jokes.setup: Jim describes Michael's current life—happily married with children in Colorado.
jokes.punchline: Michael's joy at family life is expressed through the absurd extravagance of two phones to hold all the kid photos, culminating in Jim's deadpan appreciation of the 'family plan' pun.
jokes.explanation: A warm, funny Michael joke delivered in his absence. The two phones for kid photos is recognizably Michael (excessive, oblivious to how it seems). 'He's just so happy to have a family plan' lands as both literal (phone plan) and emotional (Michael finally having a family). The wordplay feels earned rather than cheap because we know Michael's history.

jokes.text: Rules and stuff? [Said in the context of Kelly and Ryan's romantic reunion and departure]
jokes.setup: Ryan and Kelly are clearly about to run off together, abandoning his baby.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's only concern about this plan is a vague reference to 'rules and stuff'—suggesting he's briefly considered but dismissed the legal and ethical implications.
jokes.explanation: Good Ryan characterization. 'Rules and stuff' as his entire moral framework for abandoning a baby is perfectly irresponsible and perfectly Ryan. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: Ooh. Yes. Uh, they left together a little while ago. Kelly was hoping that you would keep the baby so they can start a new life together.
jokes.setup: Ravi asks for Ryan and Kelly's whereabouts.
jokes.punchline: Oscar casually reveals that Kelly has abandoned her fiancé's child — and that this was a planned, communicated intention.
jokes.explanation: Oscar's delivery of this absurdly dark information with complete composure is funny. The fact that Kelly and Ryan communicated their baby-abandonment plan while still apparently expecting it to be executed is both dark and characteristically Ryan-and-Kelly. Good economy in the revelation.

jokes.text: If Ryan wants his baby back, please tell him where to find me. We'll be somewhere in Europe.
jokes.setup: Ryan has abandoned his baby to run off with Kelly. Kevin offers the baby to Nellie.
jokes.punchline: Nellie has immediately adopted the abandoned baby and is already planning to flee to Europe with him.
jokes.explanation: Nellie's immediate adoption and European escape plan is a great character payoff. She's been established as someone who wants a child—this is a comedically dark and swift resolution. The 'somewhere in Europe' vagueness implies even she doesn't have a firm plan, but she's committed. Good dark comedy.

jokes.text: I feel like all my kids grew up and then they married each other. / It's every parent's dream!
jokes.setup: Phyllis reflects on the office family dispersing.
jokes.punchline: 'It's every parent's dream!'—as if kids growing up and marrying each other is a standard parental aspiration.
jokes.explanation: The implication that having your kids marry each other is an aspiration is the joke—it sounds vaguely incestuous. Phyllis's cheerful delivery makes it funnier. A quick, effective beat.

jokes.text: Yeah, I heard. It sounds kind of lame. No offense.
jokes.setup: Doc crew is throwing an after party. Multiple people encourage Toby to attend.
jokes.punchline: Meredith, to the doc crew's faces, says their party sounds lame—then adds 'no offense' as if that fixes it.
jokes.explanation: A quick Meredith beat. Her bluntness—to the doc crew's faces—is character-consistent. 'No offense' as a meaningless buffer is a universal joke but lands well here.

jokes.text: I need to get out of this dress. / I got to get out of this dress.
jokes.setup: Post-wedding, multiple women want out of their formal attire.
jokes.punchline: Both Angela and Pam say the exact same thing simultaneously—a small moment of unexpected solidarity between the show's most opposite characters.
jokes.explanation: A small moment of comedic synchronicity. Not particularly crafted, but the visual of Angela and Pam sharing an identical thought is a gentle character beat.

jokes.text: Well, you bought the house without telling me, so I thought I could sell it without telling you.
jokes.setup: Jim is surprised that Pam has been secretly showing their house to buyers.
jokes.punchline: Pam's logic is perfectly symmetrical and completely reasonable — the eye-for-an-eye of major undisclosed real estate decisions.
jokes.explanation: Pam's perfectly logical counter that uses Jim's own precedent against him is sharp comedy writing. The symmetry is clean, the delivery implied as dry and matter-of-fact, and the line rewards viewers who remember Jim buying the house. Strong economy and character integration — this is the culmination of Pam's growth arc delivered as a punch line.

jokes.text: I mean, you were going to do this without me? / Well, you bought the house without telling me, so I thought I could sell it without telling you.
jokes.setup: Pam reveals she's been secretly showing their house to sell it for months, to get Jim a chance to return to Athlead.
jokes.punchline: Pam defends the secrecy by pointing out Jim's own history of unilateral housing decisions.
jokes.explanation: A great line that rewards longtime viewers. Jim's purchase of the house in Scranton without Pam's knowledge was a major plot point in an earlier season. Pam invoking it here—as justification for her own secret—is both funny and a satisfying character callback. The parallelism of the phrasing is economically perfect.

jokes.text: That's why it's so clean.
jokes.setup: Pam reveals she's been showing their house for two months.
jokes.punchline: Jim's dawning realization—the house has been mysteriously clean because it was being staged for sale.
jokes.explanation: A small but well-observed beat. Jim's 'that's why it's so clean' captures the domestic comedy of a marriage—the small mysteries that suddenly make sense. Short, punchy, and feels true.

jokes.text: Oh, that's for PBS executives only. I had to pledge $50 to my local PBS station just to get this.
jokes.setup: Creed appears to try to access a restricted area or item at the party.
jokes.punchline: He claims to have pledged $50 to PBS to get access—an absurdly specific and plausible-sounding scheme that is immediately suspicious given everything we know about Creed.
jokes.explanation: A quick Creed bit. His claim to have donated to PBS is either true (he paid $50 to infiltrate a party) or a lie (which is more Creed). Either way, the specificity of $50 is funny. Works as a brief character beat.

jokes.text: Oh, um, I kind of meant just everybody from the office. [Crowd rushes to be in the photo]
jokes.setup: Pam invites everyone to take a photo in front of the mural.
jokes.punchline: Everyone—not just office people—rushes to be in the photo. Pam's clarification is too little, too late.
jokes.explanation: A quick crowd-comedy beat. Pam's belated clarification is a familiar sitcom gag but executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Very nice. Just a couple dozen more. / Smiles, everybody, smiles!
jokes.setup: The photo keeps going with everyone piling in.
jokes.punchline: 'Just a couple dozen more' being said with false enthusiasm as the photo becomes unmanageable.
jokes.explanation: A mild physical comedy beat. 'Just a couple dozen more' is a slight exaggeration but not particularly crafted. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: What the... There's only dandelion tea and raisins in here. / Hey, bottom drawer.
jokes.setup: Someone opens the office fridge expecting normal drinks.
jokes.punchline: The Dunder Mifflin fridge contains only dandelion tea and raisins—but a secret good stash is hidden in the bottom drawer.
jokes.explanation: A small but fun office-culture joke. Dandelion tea and raisins as the official fridge contents (Dwight's influence?) versus the secret bottom-drawer stash is a believable Dunder Mifflin detail. Rewards the feeling of returning home.

jokes.text: Dunder Mifflin, this is Pam. Oh, I'm sorry. Jim Halpert doesn't work here anymore.
jokes.setup: Pam alone in the office, sits at her old receptionist desk.
jokes.punchline: She instinctively answers the phone with her old greeting—then catches herself to inform the caller Jim doesn't work there. A moment of muscle memory and meta-awareness.
jokes.explanation: One of the most emotionally resonant moments in the episode, played as gentle comedy. Pam answering 'Dunder Mifflin, this is Pam' from pure habit—nine years of muscle memory—and then formally noting Jim no longer works there is both funny and moving. It encapsulates the whole episode's theme of endings and change. The laugh comes from recognition, the emotion comes from the same source. Near-perfect economy and character integration.

jokes.text: I didn't watch the whole documentary. After a few episodes, it was too painful. I kept wanting to scream at Pam.
jokes.setup: Jim reflects on watching the documentary about himself.
jokes.punchline: He couldn't watch because he kept wanting to scream at his past self to talk to Pam—a meta acknowledgment of the show's own frustrating slow-burn romance.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying meta-joke that acknowledges the audience's experience. Jim kept 'wanting to scream at Pam'—which is exactly what viewers did for seasons. The joke works because it validates the audience's frustration while also making Jim sympathetic and self-aware.

jokes.text: If there is one thing that I've learned through this whole experience, it's that if you film anybody long enough, they're going to do something stupid. / It's only human natural.
jokes.setup: Kevin shares his takeaway from being in a documentary.
jokes.punchline: 'It's only human natural'—Kevin's malapropism of 'human nature,' delivered as wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's malapropism of 'human natural' instead of 'human nature' is the perfect Kevin joke for a finale. His insight is actually correct (film anyone long enough, they'll do something dumb), but his delivery undercuts the wisdom just enough. The malapropism also lands as character-consistent and deeply endearing. 'Human natural' is one of the most quotable Kevin lines.

jokes.text: Hey, what do you say when I get back from our honeymoon, the three of us have a conference room meeting just for fun? / What is that meaningful look?
jokes.setup: Dwight proposes the three of them have a conference room meeting for fun after the honeymoon.
jokes.punchline: Jim and Pam exchange a look—they know they're about to tell Dwight they're leaving. Dwight notices the look and asks about it.
jokes.explanation: A classic Office beat—the meaningful look between Jim and Pam being noticed and called out. Dwight's 'what is that meaningful look?' is funny because he usually misses social cues entirely, but here he catches it immediately, suggesting their relationship has genuinely evolved.

jokes.text: No, don't say it. You're fired. You're both fired.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are about to tell Dwight they're leaving for Austin.
jokes.punchline: Dwight preemptively fires them to prevent them from quitting—as if being fired is preferable to being abandoned.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful finale beat. Dwight firing Jim and Pam before they can quit is a beautifully economical way to express his emotions without having to express them. It's simultaneously a power move, a defense mechanism, and a gift. The callback to Kevin's cake-firing at the episode's start adds resonance. Deeply Dwight-specific and highly quotable.

jokes.text: And, hey, if you're ever in Austin... / Oh, right, for what? The art? The music? The incredible night life? / No, thank you. / But if you're ever in the area, you'll always have a place to stay, in my barn.
jokes.setup: Jim invites Dwight to visit them in Austin.
jokes.punchline: Dwight dismisses Austin's cultural offerings, then offers them a place to stay—in his barn.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Dwight farewell joke. His dismissal of Austin's cultural appeal (art, music, nightlife—'No, thank you') and pivot to offering barn lodging captures everything about their relationship. The barn offer is Dwight's version of an open invitation—deeply sincere and completely unaware that it's not a hotel. 'There it is' as the response nail it.

jokes.text: Do I get along with my co-workers? Well, first of all, I don't have co-workers anymore. I have subordinates. So, have I gotten along with my subordinates?
jokes.setup: Dwight is asked the standard talking-head question about co-workers.
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately corrects the premise—they're subordinates, not co-workers—before answering the question.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight character comedy. His need to correct the hierarchical framing before even answering the question is pure Schrute. The pause and re-question ('So, have I gotten along with my subordinates?') is a great comedic beat.

jokes.text: My supplier relations rep, Meredith Palmer, is the only person I know who knows how to properly head bang to Motörhead.
jokes.setup: Dwight gives his final talking-head on his relationships with his subordinates.
jokes.punchline: Meredith is praised specifically for her Motörhead head-banging technique — a very specific skill Dwight has apparently evaluated.
jokes.explanation: Both Dwight and Meredith have this skill, and the specificity of Motörhead as the band (not just 'heavy metal') makes it funnier. The implication that Dwight has evaluated multiple employees' head-banging technique and Meredith is the champion is a perfectly absurd piece of character detail.

jokes.text: Angela Schrute, my former accountant, is now my wife. / My top salesman, Jim Halpert, was best man at my wedding, / and office administrator Pamela Beesly-Halpert is my best friend.
jokes.setup: Dwight lists his office relationships in professional terms.
jokes.punchline: The joke is that Dwight can only express love and friendship through workplace titles—his wife is 'former accountant,' his best friend is 'office administrator.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest character moments. Dwight categorizing his deepest personal relationships through professional titles is both funny and genuinely touching. 'Pamela Beesly-Halpert is my best friend'—the most emotionally direct thing Dwight can say, filtered through a job title—lands as one of the series' great character moments. The joke works on every level: comedy, character revelation, and emotional payoff.

jokes.text: You might feel sorry for me, but I actually feel sorry for you, because you're about to leave Cornell! So say it with me. Oh, I can so just sit here and cry!
jokes.setup: Andy is now a Cornell admissions counselor, speaking to incoming students.
jokes.punchline: Andy leads the Cornell freshmen in his own viral crying chant—reclaiming his humiliation as a rally cry.
jokes.explanation: A great arc payoff. Andy's entire episode journey—shame, humiliation, gradual redemption—culminates in him leading Cornell freshmen in his own crying chant. The inversion of the joke (humiliation → empowerment) is earned because we've watched him process it all episode. 'You're about to leave Cornell!' is a genuinely funny insight about why the frosh would relate. One of the episode's best character resolutions.

jokes.text: You did good. Real good. / Thanks, Dad. Darryl.
jokes.setup: Darryl watches Andy's triumphant moment with the Cornell students.
jokes.punchline: 'Thanks, Dad.' Andy accidentally calls Darryl 'Dad,' then quickly corrects to 'Darryl'—but the slip says everything about their friendship.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully small moment. 'Thanks, Dad. Darryl.' is four words that encapsulate Andy's need for paternal approval and the genuine bond he's found at Dunder Mifflin. The quick self-correction makes it funnier and sadder simultaneously. One of the episode's most quotable beats.

jokes.text: I wish there was a way to know you're in the good old days before you've actually left them. / Someone should write a song about that.
jokes.setup: Andy delivers a genuinely moving observation about nostalgia.
jokes.punchline: 'Someone should write a song about that'—a gentle, self-aware acknowledgment that this is the kind of sentiment that becomes a pop song, slightly undercutting the earnestness.
jokes.explanation: The observation itself is one of the series' most beloved lines. The 'someone should write a song about that' functions as both a gentle joke (treating his own insight as a casual idea) and meta-commentary (it's already a song, in a sense). The comedy is subtle—it's more emotional resonance than laugh—but it earns its place as a comedy beat.

jokes.text: But seriously, you made a nine-year documentary and you couldn't once show me doing my origami?
jokes.setup: Various characters reflect on the documentary and what it showed/didn't show of their lives.
jokes.punchline: After all of Creed's nine-year mysteries—the Grass Roots, the drugs, the weapons-grade LSD—his complaint about the documentary is that they didn't show his origami hobby.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Creed joke and one of the episode's very best moments. After we've learned Creed is a drug trafficker, endangered species meat dealer, and military LSD thief—after he faked his own death—his one grievance with the documentary is the omission of his origami practice. The mundanity of the complaint against the backdrop of his criminal insanity is the whole joke. The specificity of 'origami' (not 'hobbies' or 'good things about me') is perfect. This is close to the caliber of the snip-snap anchor example—deeply character-specific, surprising, quotable, and earned by nine seasons of Creed mythology.

jokes.text: Oscar? Oscar? / I think I'm gay. / Why do you say that? / It's just that I'm so emotional. / You're not gay. You're not gay.
jokes.setup: Kevin calls out to Oscar at the party, clearly emotional.
jokes.punchline: Kevin tells Oscar he thinks he's gay because he's emotional. Oscar denies it. The joke is Kevin's logic (emotional = gay) and Oscar's slightly defensive insistence.
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully unexpected character beat. Kevin's logic—being emotional at the party means he might be gay, and Oscar would know—is both naive and sweet. Oscar's slightly too-emphatic denial ('You're not gay. You're not gay.') adds a funny layer. The exchange works because it's earnest from Kevin and flustered from Oscar. A late-episode gem.

jokes.text: How did you capture what it was really like? How we felt, and how we made each other laugh, and how we got through the day. How did you do it? / Also how do cameras work?
jokes.setup: Darryl gives a heartfelt speech to the documentary crew about how they captured the essence of Dunder Mifflin.
jokes.punchline: Creed follows the emotional question with 'Also how do cameras work?'—which is either genuine ignorance or perfect comedic timing.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. Darryl's genuine, emotional question—building beautifully through three 'How did you...' beats—is perfectly punctured by Creed immediately following with 'Also how do cameras work?' It's the quintessential Office joke: emotional sincerity immediately deflated by absurdist non-sequitur. Creed's follow-up question being completely literal and technologically basic is both funny and consistent with his mysterious, possibly-time-displaced character.

jokes.text: I worked for a paper company all these years, and I never wrote anything down.
jokes.setup: Pam reflects on the documentary capturing memories she'd otherwise have lost.
jokes.punchline: She spent nine years at a paper company and never wrote anything down—a gentle, self-aware irony.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best observational jokes. The irony of a paper company employee never writing anything down is perfect—simple, specific, and deeply true about the show's world. It works as both a joke and a genuine insight about memory and documentation. The economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: This stupid, wonderful, boring, amazing job.
jokes.setup: Dwight reflects on his career at Dunder Mifflin.
jokes.punchline: The contradictory adjective pairs—stupid/wonderful, boring/amazing—capture the show's whole ethos in four words. The comedy is in the structure (stupid before wonderful, boring before amazing).
jokes.explanation: The best closing line in the episode. 'This stupid, wonderful, boring, amazing job' encapsulates The Office's entire thesis—that ordinary work lives contain extraordinary meaning—in eight words. The comedy is in the structure: insult first, compliment second, each time. It's also a joke about the show's own premise (a boring, stupid documentary about a paper company that turned out to be wonderful and amazing). One of the most quotable lines in the entire series run. The economy is perfect—not one unnecessary word.

tmdb_overview: One year later, Dunder Mifflin employees past and present reunite for a panel discussion about the documentary and to attend Dwight and Angela's wedding.
